title: Address and data generators
summary: A March element needs an **address** for every step and the right **data** for every write and expected read. Two small generators produce them: an up/down address counter and a data-background generator.
objectives: Explain how one up/down counter produces both ⇑ and ⇓.
Explain fast-row and fast-column order and why address scrambling matters.
Produce solid, checkerboard and stripe data from the background and the address bits.
Describe what write masks and different word widths add to the generators.

steps.title: One counter
steps.md: An n-bit counter (2ⁿ ≥ N) with a **direction** input. The controller loads the first address, then steps the counter once per address.
Load 0 and count up. When the counter reaches N−1, the comparator signals **last address** and the element ends.
Load N−1 and count down to 0 — exactly the reverse order, as March tests require.

steps.title: Rows and columns
steps.md: The address is made of **row bits** (which word line) and **column bits** (which column of the multiplexer). Which part counts fastest sets the visiting order.

blocks.title: Memories that are not a power of two
blocks.md: A memory with 1000 words needs a 10-bit counter that stops at 999, not at 1023. The **last address** is a parameter of each memory — so one shared counter can serve memories of different sizes.

rows: stays on one word line and walks through its columns — stresses column multiplexers and bit lines
changes the word line every access — stresses row decoders and word-line switching
blocks.caption: Two common address orders; good MBIST runs critical algorithms in both

steps.title: Fast column
steps.md: Counting the **column** bits fastest walks along one word line, then moves to the next.

steps.title: Fast row
steps.md: Counting the **row** bits fastest changes the word line on every access.

steps.title: Scrambling
steps.md: In the layout, logical rows may be swapped or folded. Physical neighbours are then not logical neighbours.

blocks.md:
The **logical** address (what the controller counts) is not always the **physical** position of the cell: memory designers fold arrays, mirror halves and interleave bits to save area. This mapping is called **address scrambling** (and **data scrambling** for bits).

Most March tests do not care — they visit every address in some order and its reverse. But tests that depend on **physical neighbours** — checkerboard, neighbourhood patterns, row/column stripes — need the scrambling information from the memory vendor, and the generator applies it.

blocks.prompt: Practice: a memory has 2 rows and 2 columns. Put the addresses in **fast-column** order.

blocks.md:
The data generator turns the **0 / 1** of the March test into a word:

> data = background D, inverted when the operation says 1 (w1, r1)

Patterns that depend on the position of the cell are made by XOR-ing the background with **address bits**:

rows: every cell differs from its 4 neighbours
blocks.caption: Address-dependent data with one XOR gate per pattern (physical address bits)
Four patterns from one background and two address bits

blocks.title: Expected data comes from the same generator
blocks.md: For a read, the generator produces the data that *should* be in the cell; this is the **expected data** sent to the comparator. One generator serves both writes and compares.

items.title: Byte-write enables (write masks)
items.md: Many memories can write only some bytes of a word. MBIST must test this logic too: write with a byte **masked**, read back, and check that the masked byte did **not** change.

items.title: Different word widths
items.md: A shared controller may serve a 16-bit and a 72-bit memory. The data generator makes a pattern for the widest one; each collar takes the bits it needs. The background repeats across the word (e.g. 0101… for every width).

items.title: Data backgrounds
items.md: The background register is loaded with D0, D1 … in turn (log₂(B) + 1 of them), and the whole March test is repeated for each — exactly as in *March Tests*, Topic 5.

questions.text: How does an MBIST address generator produce a ⇓ element?
options: It loads N−1 and counts down to 0.
It counts up and the memory reverses the addresses.
It reads the addresses from the tester.

questions.text: A shared controller tests a 1000-word and a 4096-word memory. What does it need for each memory?
Why does a checkerboard test need the memory's address scrambling information?
options: Logical neighbours are not always physical neighbours, and the checkerboard is about physical neighbours.
Without it the memory cannot be written.
It does not — scrambling only matters for ROMs.

questions.text: Which expression gives checkerboard data from background D?
In fast-column order the test stays on one word line while it walks through the columns.
How is a byte-write enable tested?
options: Write with one byte masked and check that the masked byte did not change.
It cannot be tested by MBIST.
